source_text: Οὐκ εἶπεν ,,οἡμέρα πρώτη“. εἰ γὰρ πρώτην ἡμέραν εἶπεν, ἀνάγκὴν εἶχεν εἰπεῖν καὶ δευτέραν γινομένην. ἀλλ᾽ ἔδει μὴ πρώτην λέγειν ἀλλὰ ο,,μίων“, ἵνα διὰ τοῦ ,,μίαν““ εἰπεῖν ταύτην δείξῃ κυκλουμένην ὅ καὶ ἑβδομάδα διατελοῦσαν, μίαν δὲ ὑπάρχουσαν.
pass_a_gloss: He did not say 'first day'. For if He said 'first day', it was necessary for Him to say also 'second day' coming to be. But it was necessary for Him not to say 'first' but 'one', so that through the 'one' He might show this day being cyclical, and also the week being completed, and it being one.
pass_b_english: He did not say "first day." If He had said "first day," He would have been compelled to say "second day" as it came into being. Instead, He had to say not "first" but "one," so that by using "one" He could show this day as cyclical, and the week as completed, yet still a single unit.

anf_compare.notes: Drafted from source only; ANF not shown to drafter.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek nuances regarding the distinction between 'first' (πρώτην) and 'one' (μίαν), preserving the causal logic of the necessity (ἀνάγκὴν εἶχεν) and the cyclical/completeness arguments (κυκλουμένην, διατελοῦσαν).
